paras: The lynching in Claiborne County, Mississippi, was the punishment of an unnamed Black man accused of rape by "Judge Lynch" in the week before May 5, 1888. It is known from a single sentence in the Grenada Sentinel, which paired it with a lynching at Vicksburg and did not say what was done to the man.

In its issue of May 5, 1888, the Sentinel stated that "Judge Lynch" had "paid his respects in Vicksburg and in Claiborne county during the past week on two negroes for committing rape." The only further detail concerned Vicksburg, where the act took place "in front of the court house door." For Claiborne County the paper gave no name, town, date, method or number of participants, and it did not state that the man was killed, although "Judge Lynch" was the usual newspaper term for mob punishment.
No report of an arrest, inquest or other official response appears in the coverage.

The Sentinel ran the sentence without a byline or source in a column of clipped items from other papers, set between a paragraph credited to the Picayune and another signed "N. O. Picayune," so its origin is uncertain. The item used the jocular idiom of "Judge Lynch" paying "his respects," stated the accusation of rape as fact, and offered no comment. No other report of the Claiborne County case, local or wire, appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Lynching in Claiborne County, Mississippi (1888)
bases: A1 says "Judge Lynch" paid his respects in Claiborne county to a negro for committing rape, the standard newspaper phrase for mob punishment, paired with a Vicksburg case that other papers call a lynching (A2, A3).

A1's "Judge Lynch" phrasing marks extralegal mob punishment of a man accused of rape, but it does not state that he was killed, how, or by how many; the paired Vicksburg case was a lynching by other reports (A2, A3), which makes a killing likely but not stated.
One unattributed paragraph in A1 is the only report of the Claiborne County case; A2, A3 and A5 corroborate only the Vicksburg case it names alongside.
